title: ViTSP: Vision Language Models Guide Large-Scale TSP
one_liner: A framework uses a pre-trained image-understanding model to spot promising regions in a drawn map of cities, then runs a classical solver on those pieces to find better routes for thousands or tens of thousands of stops.
lead: The Traveling Salesman Problem asks: what is the shortest route that visits every city once and returns home? With thousands of cities, the problem explodes — there are more possible routes than atoms in the universe. Classical solvers bog down, heuristic tweaks require expert tuning, and neural models trained on one city set fail on another. ViTSP sidesteps training by borrowing a pre-trained image-understanding model (one that already learned to recognize shapes and patterns in pictures) to look at a visual map and spot the promising small pieces. These pieces get solved cleanly with a classical optimizer, and the pieces are stitched together into a whole-map solution.

problem.h2: Three methods, none scale to real-world size
paras: Classical exact solvers (algorithms that find the mathematically best route) are beautifully precise but grind to a halt with 10,000 cities. They explore too many possibilities.

Heuristic methods (hand-designed shortcuts that find good-enough routes fast) work at scale but require an expert to tune their parameters for each problem type — change the city layout or the cost model, and the tuning fails.

Learning-based methods (neural networks trained on examples) run fast and need no manual tuning, but they learn only the patterns in their training data. Show them a new city set or a much larger one, and they flounder — the patterns have shifted.

callout.b: The trap: three solutions, but none handle both large scale and unfamiliar layouts.
callout.html: Use a pre-trained image model to visually identify small high-quality chunks of the big map, then solve those chunks cleanly and assemble the global solution.

steps.text: Draw the cities as points on an image or heatmap.
Feed the image into a pre-trained vision language model (a neural net that has already learned to understand pictures and text together from billions of examples).

steps.b: Step 3: Ask the model for clusters
steps.text: Use the model's internal understanding to identify regions that cluster together or form natural subproblems.
Run a classical exact solver (like LKH-3) on each small-scale cluster; these solvers are fast enough on 50-500 cities.
Chain the optimal local tours together into a global tour covering all cities.

paras: Instead of training a custom neural network or manually tuning parameters, the paper shifts the burden onto visual understanding. It borrows a model that already knows how to see and interpret patterns (trained on images and descriptions), applies that model to a map representation of the cities, and uses the model's judgment to partition the problem into solvable pieces.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: cluster quality and cohesion
hidden.name: How well the vision model partitions the cities
paras: The paper does not explicitly measure a single number called 'cluster quality,' but its core success hinges on whether the vision model identifies clusters of cities that are genuinely close together and naturally form a good local tour.

The paper estimates this implicitly by checking if the final tours are short. A vision model that carves the map into poor clusters — like putting far-apart cities in the same group — will fail at the root: the downstream solver cannot fix a fundamentally bad partition. So the paper's measure of cluster quality is indirect: the quality of the final tour reveals whether the visual partitioning was sound.

heat.caption: Darker means more important to final tour quality. High values in city clusters and vision recognition drive better results.

reads.html: Watch: does the vision model put all close-together cities into the same cluster, or does it scramble them? If it gets the partition right, even a simple greedy solver will succeed.
The paper's core bet is that transfer learning (using a model pre-trained on billions of images and text) captures enough spatial reasoning to partition a new unseen TSP instance correctly.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: reuse learned vision over training from scratch
paras: A neural network trained only on small TSP instances (say, up to 1,000 cities) has learned patterns specific to that training range. Show it 10,000 cities and it chokes because the distribution has shifted — the model's internal weights are tuned to the old pattern.

A pre-trained vision language model, by contrast, has been exposed to billions of real-world images and learned general shape-recognition, clustering, and spatial reasoning. When you show it a new TSP map (even one with vastly more cities), its learned intuition about how things cluster together in space transfers directly, because the visual pattern is the same: dense regions and sparse regions look the same regardless of whether there are 100 or 10,000 cities.

Classical solvers are brittle but optimal at small scales. By partitioning the big map into small clusters (each solvable by a classical solver), the framework avoids the explosion of the search space while keeping the optimality guarantee within each cluster. The final tour is not globally optimal, but it is locally optimal in every piece.

stages.s: pre-trained vision model extracts spatial patterns
classical solver optimizes each cluster exactly

math.h2: The cost formula: travel distance plus partition penalty
math.words: total_tour_length = sum of distances along the route + small penalty if clusters are poorly stitched
math.equation: L_total = sum_edges dist(city_i, city_j) + lambda * penalty(cluster_junctions)
symbols: the total tour length in distance units
the straight-line distance between city i and city j
add up all the jumps along the tour
a small weight; how much we penalize poor stitching between clusters
extra distance incurred when jumping from one cluster to another

worked.title: A tiny worked example: three clusters, stitching cost
lines: Cluster A has 50 cities; internal tour distance = 150 units.
Cluster B has 60 cities; internal tour distance = 180 units.
Cluster C has 40 cities; internal tour distance = 120 units.
Jump from A to B = 10 units. Jump from B to C = 15 units. Jump C back to start = 8 units.
If lambda = 0.1 and junctions are poor, penalty adds maybe 5 units -> final 488.
If the vision model identifies clusters well, junctions are natural and penalty is near zero.

math.note: The classical solver finds the best path within each cluster, and the vision model's partition minimizes wasted distance at cluster boundaries.

charts.title: Learning-based baseline (fixed network)
charts.note: Networks trained on small data fail catastrophically on large, new-shaped instances. Optimality gap grows with problem size.

charts.title: Classical heuristic (LKH-3, hand-tuned)
charts.note: Reliable across sizes but requires domain expertise to tune. Slower on very large instances.

charts.title: ViTSP (vision-guided, no training needed)
charts.note: Sub-0.2% gap on all sizes. No per-problem tuning. Vision model transfer eliminates the need to retrain.

items.b: Vision model misses the true structure.
items.html: If the map has an unusual layout (cities arranged in a thin spiral, or in a fractal pattern the vision model has never seen), the model's partitioning may be wrong. For example, it might group far-apart cities because they appear visually adjacent in the compressed visualization.

If the vision model cuts the map in a way that splits tight groups apart, the inter-cluster jumps will be long and wasteful. The local optimal tours within clusters cannot recover from a bad global partition.
TSP cost may not be Euclidean distance (e.g., driving distance over roads). If the visual representation does not match the cost model, the vision model's spatial reasoning becomes irrelevant.

items.b: Done right: vision models trained on real-world maps and layouts.
items.html: When the pre-trained model has seen similar spatial distributions during pre-training, it transfers its understanding directly. No retraining, no domain tuning, just borrowed insight from a bigger teacher.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small working instance: generate 500 cities scattered on a 1000-by-1000 grid, with a known optimal tour (or a known near-optimal solution from LKH-3). Feed a visualization of that instance to a pre-trained vision language model (you can use a freely available model like CLIP or Qwen-VL). Extract what the model considers to be interesting regions or clusters by asking it to annotate regions, or by measuring which parts of the image the model spent the most internal effort thinking about (the model's focus). Partition the 500 cities into 3-5 clusters based on the model's output. Run an exact solver on each cluster. Stitch the cluster tours together. Measure the final tour length and compare it to the optimal (the gap as a percentage). The demo must show that a pre-trained model's visual intuition produces a reasonable partition without any training on TSP examples.
demo.metric_eq: optimality_gap (shown as a percentage of the optimal distance)
demo.closing: The metric must show that the vision-guided partition produces a sub-1% gap on a 500-city instance in a single forward pass (no retraining) and that naive neural methods or random partitions fail by comparison.
